records.sourceFile: How Humans Run Faster - The Neuromechanical Contributions of Functional Muscle Groups to Running at Different Speeds.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Laboratory study of 11 male middle-distance runners who ran on an instrumented treadmill at six speeds from 2.78 to 8.33 m/s, with kinematics, ground reaction forces, EMG and inverse-dynamics work by muscle group. Ankle plantar flexors were the largest contributor to stance work at all speeds, but hip extensors and knee flexors dominated whole-stride work at higher speeds. Plantar flexor stance kinetics explained 96-97% of the variance in step length, and hip extensor swing kinetics explained 98-99% of the variance in step frequency.
records.limitations: The sample is 11 men from one event group, and the top speed (8.33 m/s) is below elite sprint speed. Work by muscle group is inferred from net joint moments, and EMG covered eight muscles with some reduced sample sizes.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the step-length and step-frequency relationships as proof that training one muscle group will change stride mechanics, when the study only shows associations within one treadmill protocol.

records.sourceFile: Human foot muscle strength and its association with sprint acceleration, cutting and jumping performance, and kinetics in high-level athletes.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Cross-sectional study of 52 injury-free, high-level athletes (5 women; soccer, rugby, track and field, basketball and handball; mean age 20.1 years) who completed a maximal isometric metatarsophalangeal (MTP) flexion torque test, then sprint, cutting and jump tests on force platforms. MTP pushing and total torque correlated moderately with 10 m sprint time in the high-acceleration condition (r = -0.33) and with vertical impulse and contact time at maximal speed, and models combining MTP torque with foot deformation or foot-ankle reactive strength explained 28% and 35% of variance in those maximal-speed kinetics.
records.limitations: This is a correlational, single-session study in mostly young male athletes, with single-angle isometric tests and no hip strength measure. Many correlations were non-significant or small to moderate, and the authors note the study may be underpowered.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff may read the MTP flexion correlations as proof that training forefoot strength will improve sprinting, when the study measured associations only and did not train anyone.

changes: evidenceSummary, abstract, findings: 26% to 38% was described as variance explained in MTP-related outcomes and in models including MTP torque -> 26% to 38% applies to jump models; MTP torque was retained only in the maximal-speed (28%, 35%) and horizontal-jump models; acceleration (MIPFt + MIQt, 27% to 36%) and cutting (MIPFt, reactive strength, foot posture, 35%) models did not include it
findings: gripping torque vs horizontal jump power given without direction -> negative association ('(i.e., lower performance) for gripping torque')
findings: added that no MTP variable related to cutting time (COD r = -0.25, p = 0.08)
limitations: kept the 37% (Discussion) vs adjusted r2 0.35 (Results) conflict and added the vertical jump 23%/26% vs 26% to 38% inconsistency
practicalImplications: quadriceps torque was said to relate to cutting -> it contributed to acceleration and jumping; plantarflexor torque to acceleration and cutting
tldr: 'some sprint times' and weaker cutting link -> 10 m high-acceleration time only; no cutting association; negative gripping-horizontal jump link
sports: added the five sampled sports

records.sourceFile: Hypoxia and resistance exercise - a comparison of     localized and systemic methods.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Narrative review of resistance exercise combined with blood flow restriction (BFR) and with systemic hypoxia (intermittent hypoxic resistance training, IHRT). IHRT evidence is limited to a few studies, including one 5-week study of 30 female netball athletes (Manimmanakorn et al.). The authors conclude that low-intensity BFR training can produce greater muscle and strength gains than equivalent training without BFR, and that IHRT cannot yet support firm recommendations.
records.limitations: No systematic search or study-quality appraisal is described, so study selection and the strength of each claim cannot be checked. Most mechanisms discussed (metabolite accumulation, growth hormone, cell swelling, ROS) are hypotheses drawn largely from BFR and animal work.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the proposed mechanisms as established causes of hypertrophy, when the authors describe most of them as unclear, equivocal or speculative.

records.sourceFile: Impact of Blood Flow Restriction                                Exercise on Muscle Fatigue Development and            Recovery.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Randomized, counterbalanced, within-subject laboratory study of 17 healthy, physically active, resistance-trained males (mean age 25 years). Each completed four sets of low-intensity knee extension (30 percent 1RM) with blood flow restriction (BFR, 60 percent of arterial occlusion pressure) and without BFR. Maximal voluntary torque (MVT) fell 44.5 percent with BFR and 24.3 percent in control at exercise termination, and twitch torque recovered substantially within 2 minutes of cuff release.
records.limitations: The sample was male only, small (n = 17), and not described as athletes. Acute neuromuscular changes after one session do not show training adaptations, and peripheral nerve stimulation cannot separate spinal from supraspinal causes of central fatigue.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the fast twitch recovery after BFR as proof that BFR is safe to repeat every session, when the study measured one session and found maximal torque had not fully recovered after 8 minutes.

changes: paper.citation: author 'Mittelmeier' -> 'Mittlmeier' (as printed).
evidenceSummary/abstract: added 'resistance-trained' ('Seventeen resistance-trained males'; resistance training at least twice per week).
paper.tldr: 'Most of the difference disappears within 2 minutes' -> MVT group difference gone by 2 min, but SS and PS10:PS100 differences persisted through recovery and PS100 to 4 min.
paper.practicalImplications: 'twitch torque loss recovers within about 2 minutes' -> 'much of the torque loss recovers within minutes', noting MVT still 13.4% down at 8 min.

records.sourceFile: Impact of hip flexion angle on unilateral and bilateral Nordic hamstring exercise torque and high density electromyography activity.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Laboratory study of 13 amateur male football and rugby players (mean age 23 +/- 3 years) who performed bilateral and unilateral Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) with neutral hips (NHE0) and with 90-degree hip flexion (NHE90) at an eccentric 1-repetition maximum load. Knee flexion torque and high-density EMG of the biceps femoris long head (BFLH) and semitendinosus (ST) were compared with statistical parametric mapping. NHE90 produced higher torque and lower EMG than NHE0 in both muscles, and unilateral and bilateral modes gave similar peak torque and EMG when load was matched.
records.limitations: The sample is small (n = 13) and amateur, and the authors state that false negatives and biased effect sizes are possible. The study measured acute torque and EMG in one session, so it cannot show training adaptations or injury outcomes.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the higher torque and lower EMG in NHE90 as proof that it is the safer or more protective version, but the study did not measure adaptation or injury rates.

changes: paper.limitations: omitted device conflict of interest and dominant-leg-only recording -> added ('Jean-Patrick Giacomo is the inventor and patent owner of the hamstring testing load-cell device used in this study'; 'Torque (Newton meters) for the dominant leg')

records.sourceFile: Improving strength and power in trained athletes with 3     weeks of occlusion training.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Randomized, counterbalanced crossover trial in 20 male semiprofessional rugby union players (mean age 21.5 years, at least 2 years of resistance training) who each completed two 3-week preseason blocks of 5 x 5 bench press, squat and weighted pull-up at 70% 1RM, one with and one without intermittent 180 mmHg occlusion of both thighs. The authors report greater gains with occlusion in bench press (5.4 vs 3.3 kg), squat (7.8 vs 4.3 kg), best 40 m sprint time (-0.03 vs -0.01 s), countermovement-jump power and repeated-sprint maintenance, with larger acute salivary testosterone responses and an acute cortisol response that was attenuated across the occlusion block.
records.limitations: Twenty players from one club in one preseason is a small sample, the two 3-week blocks ran back to back within an 8-week preseason with no washout described, and the outcomes were strength, sprint and jump tests rather than muscle size or sport performance. Some absolute gains were small (sprint time improved by 0.03 vs 0.01 s).
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the bench press gain after lower-body occlusion as proof of a systemic training effect that transfers to upper-body strength, when the study is one small crossover in one squad and the authors frame the mechanism and the testosterone link as suggestive, not causal.

records.sourceFile: Is it a slow day or a go day - The perceptions and applications of velocity-based training within elite strength and conditioning.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Qualitative study using semi-structured remote interviews with 14 male high-performance strength and conditioning coaches (not athletes), analysed with reflexive thematic analysis. Three central themes were reported: technology (drivers for buying devices), applications (testing, monitoring, programming and feedback) and reflections (benefits, drawbacks and future use). Coaches valued velocity-based training for objective prescription, readiness tracking and intent, and cited cost, set-up time, erroneous data and chasing velocity as drawbacks.
records.limitations: The sample is 14 male coaches, mostly from the UK, USA and Australia, recruited by purposive and opportunity sampling, so the findings describe these practitioners' views and are not measures of athlete outcomes. The principal investigator is a VBT researcher and practising coach, and the data are self-reported interview accounts rather than observed practice.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read coaches' reported uses of velocity-based training as evidence that these methods improve outcomes, when the study reports practitioner perceptions and does not test effectiveness.

records.sourceFile: Kinematics and kinetics of pick-up acceleration.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Narrative review of gait-transition and sprint biomechanics literature on accelerating from a submaximal entry (walking, jogging or running). The authors define pickup acceleration, propose a step framework (approach steps -2 and -1, transition step 0, pickup steps 1 and 2), and summarize kinematic and kinetic data that come mostly from small studies. They report that the transition step gives the largest step-to-step velocity increase (up to about 30 percent from walking), with accelerations of 2.62 to 3.63 m/s2.
records.limitations: No database search strategy or appraisal of study quality is described. The normative values come from small samples, and the review notes that the cited walking-entry studies used small groups (9 to 17) of female subjects with no stated athletic background.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat the walking-entry values as benchmarks for their own athletes, when the review says jogging-entry kinetics are largely unstudied and that the cited studies used different entry methods.

changes: paper.citation: running-header placeholder volume '0(0)' removed; only year and pages 1-9 are printed for this online article

paper.findings: '34 percent increase on the transition step' reworded to 'from the transition step' ('a 34% increase from the previous step'); ranking claim attributed to the authors' own Figure 1 testing
screeningLimitations: tightened wording on the 9 to 17 female subjects ('small groups (9-17) of female subjects, with no mention of an athletic background')
verification.residualConcerns: The rank-order data in Figure 1 come from the authors' unpublished testing with mixed sport athletes and are presented without sample details.
